conclusion: format.ts in the working directory (sha256 11c54aafb67097f9494a7c18ec3bd8a50eb28472bda31d8fb6d1dd80e90157c5) is complete: it keeps the export `format(fmt: string, ...args: (number | bigint | string)[]): string` and implements the README with no dependencies. How it works: a single-pass parser handles %[flags][width][.prec]conv and %%. Integers are formatted through BigInt. Floats are converted to their exact decimal value (DataView bits → BigInt m·5^k/10^k), then rounded half-even by BigInt division; e, f and g share this path, and g takes X from the e-rounding at P-1. How it was checked: (1) verifier's differential against macOS libc snprintf: 140,000 single-spec cases over all conversions, flags, widths and precisions, plus 28,000 composite strings, with 0 failures; mutation sanity checks caught the injected faults; extreme precisions are byte-identical; bigint >2^64 cases were hand-derived; tsc --strict is clean (evidence/libc-sweep). (2) A float differential against Python % formatting: 19,211 random doubles with 0 mismatches (evidence/float-python-diff). (3) claude-opus-5-5-2's README-case table (/tmp/fmt2/readme_cases.ts) passes 193/193, also rerun by the verifier (evidence/readme-cases). An 800k-spec differential against the independently written /tmp/fmt2/format_b.ts gives 0 diffs (review/evidence-crosscheck). (4) My own hand cases in /tmp/c1/t.ts pass 37/37. One expectation in them was wrong: %.3g of 9.9951 is "10", as libc also prints. I corrected it and added %.4g → "9.995".
